=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Statistics 2025 Question 4 (4 points total).
Topic: Focus on Inference (One-Sample z-Test for a Population Proportion).
Problem Context: In Country W, 22% of high school students use a homework app weekly. Karen surveys an SRS of n = 130 students from her high school (N > 2,000) and finds 38 use the app (p_hat = 38/130 = 0.2923). Test if the proportion at her school is greater than 0.22 at alpha = 0.05.
Rubric Expectations:
- Section 1 (Hypotheses & Identification): (1) Identify one-sample z-test for proportion; (2) State H0: p = 0.22; (3) State Ha: p > 0.22; (4) Define p in context with population descriptor ('true proportion of students at Karen's high school who use the app weekly'). [Scored E/P/I]
- Section 2 (Conditions & Mechanics): (1) Verify random sample of 130 and 10% condition (130 <= 0.10(2000)); (2) Large counts check using p0 = 0.22: np0 = 130(0.22) = 28.6 >= 10 and n(1-p0) = 130(0.78) = 101.4 >= 10; (3) Calculate z = (0.2923 - 0.22)/sqrt(0.22*0.78/130) = 1.99; (4) Calculate p-value = P(z >= 1.99) = 0.0233. [Scored E/P/I]
- Section 3 (Conclusion): (1) Compare p-value (0.0233) < alpha (0.05) and reject H0; (2) State non-definitive conclusion in context supporting that the true proportion of students at Karen's school using the app is greater than 0.22. [Scored E/P/I]

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 4A) ===
1 sample z test for p
p = the true proportion of high school students at Karen's school that use the app to help them with their homework at least once a week.
Ho: p = 0.22; Ha: p > 0.22; alpha = 0.05
Conditions: Random: Karen chose a random sample of 130 students at her school. 10% condition: 130 <= 0.1(2,000), 2000 = all students at Karen's school. Large counts condition: 0.22(130) = 28.6 >= 10; 0.78(130) = 101.4 >= 10. Since all conditions are met we can perform a 1 sample z test for p.
Mechanics: z = (0.2923 - 0.22) / sqrt((0.22 * 0.78) / 130) = 1.9902; P(Z >= 1.9902) = 0.02328
Conclusion: Since the p value of 0.02328 < 0.05, we reject Ho, and have convincing evidence for Ha, that the true proportion of students at Karen's school that use the app to help them with homework at least once a week is greater than 0.22.
feedback:
Total Score: 4/4 points (Complete Response: Section 1 - E, Section 2 - E, Section 3 - E).
- Section 1 [E]: Named one-sample z-test for proportion, stated correct one-sided hypotheses with p = 0.22, and defined parameter with 'true proportion' in full context.
- Section 2 [E]: Verified random sampling, 10% rule (130 <= 200), and expected large counts (28.6 and 101.4 >= 10), reporting accurate z = 1.99 and p-value = 0.0233.
- Section 3 [E]: Compared p-value to alpha, correctly rejected H0, and stated a non-definitive conclusion in full context.

State: 1 prop z test. Ho: p = 0.22; Ha: p > 0.22; alpha = 0.05; p_hat = 38/130 = 0.292. p = true proportion of all students at Karen's school who use the app to help them with their homework at least once per week.
Plan: random sample of 130 students from Karen's school; (130)(0.292) = 37.96 >= 10; (130)(1 - 0.292) = 92.04 >= 10; Normal distribution: 130 > 30.
Do: z = (0.292 - 0.22) / sqrt((0.292 * (1 - 0.292)) / 130) = 1.9902 -> p-value = 1 - 0.9767 = 0.0233.
Conclude: The p-value of 0.0233 is lower than the alpha of 0.05 so we reject the null hypothesis, there is convincing evidence that the proportion of students at Karen's school who use the app to help them with their homework at least once per week is greater than the proportion of her country.

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Statistics 2025 Question 5 (4 points total).
Topic: Multi-Focus (Discrete Probability Distribution, Expected Value, Hypotheses, Type I Error & Confidence Interval Decision).
Problem Context: 2024 sample of newly built houses in Country B: 1 bed (0.12), 2 bed (0.22), 3 bed (0.28), 4 bed (0.22), 5 bed (0.14), 6 bed (0.02). 2017 baseline mean was 2.9 bedrooms. 97% confidence interval for 2024 mean is (3.01, 3.19).
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A: (i) P(X < 3) = P(1) + P(2) = 0.12 + 0.22 = 0.34; (ii) E(X) = 1(0.12) + 2(0.22) + 3(0.28) + 4(0.22) + 5(0.14) + 6(0.02) = 3.10 bedrooms. [Needs 3 of 4 for E]
- Part B: (i) H0: mu = 2.9 vs. Ha: mu != 2.9, where mu is the population mean number of bedrooms in newly built houses in 2024 from Country B; (ii) Type I Error: Concluding the population mean number of bedrooms is not 2.9 when in reality it is 2.9. [Needs 4 of 4 for E]
- Part C: (1) State null hypothesis is rejected because 2.9 is not contained in the 97% confidence interval (3.01, 3.19); (2) Conclude convincing statistical evidence at alpha = 0.03 that the true mean number of bedrooms in 2024 differs from 2.9. [Needs 2 of 2 for E]

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 5A) ===
A) i. P(Bedrooms < 3) = 0.12 + 0.22 = 0.34.
ii. mu = 1(0.12) + 2(0.22) + 3(0.28) + 4(0.22) + 5(0.14) + 6(0.02) = 3.1 bedrooms.
B) i. Let mu = the true mean number of bedrooms in newly built houses in the country in 2024. Ho: mu = 2.9; Ha: mu != 2.9.
ii. The true mean number of bedrooms in 2024 is 2.9 bedrooms, but there was convincing statistical evidence supporting the alternative that the mean was not 2.9 bedrooms.
C) The null hypothesis can be rejected since 2.9 is not within the confidence interval. There is enough evidence to suggest that the true mean number of bedrooms in 2024 is not 2.9 bedrooms.
feedback:
Total Score: 4/4 points (Complete Response: Part A - E, Part B - E, Part C - E).
- Part A [E]: Correctly calculated P(X < 3) = 0.34 and expected value E(X) = 3.10 bedrooms with complete supporting summation.
- Part B [E]: Stated two-sided hypotheses for mu = 2.9 with full parameter context, and accurately defined a Type I error in context.
- Part C [E]: Justified rejection of H0 because 2.9 is outside the (3.01, 3.19) interval, concluding with non-definitive language in context.

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Statistics 2025 Question 6 (4 points total).
Topic: Investigative Task (Two-Sample t-Test vs. Paired t-Test & Cohen's d Effect Size Analysis).
Problem Context: Stefan studies reading comprehension scores of 100 children randomly assigned to read at 9 a.m. (n1 = 50, x_bar1 = 15.2, s1 = 4.12) or 3 p.m. (n2 = 50, x_bar2 = 17.9, s2 = 4.43). Two-sample t-test yields t = -3.15, p-value = 0.002.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A (Inference Conclusion): (1) Compare p-value (0.002) < alpha (0.05) and reject H0; (2) Conclude convincing statistical evidence of a difference in mean reading scores between children reading at 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. using non-definitive language in context. [Scored E/P/I]
- Part B (Design Choice): (1) State two-sample t-test is appropriate because groups are independent / not paired; (2) Explain independence via random assignment to separate groups / absence of matching (e.g., twins or testing each child twice). [Scored E/P/I]
- Part C (Effect Size Calculation): (i) Pooled SD s_p = sqrt((4.12^2 + 4.43^2)/2) = 4.28 -> Cohen's d = |15.2 - 17.9| / 4.28 = 0.63; (ii) Interpret from Table 2: d = 0.63 indicates results are 'somewhat practical / meaningful in real life'. [Scored E/P/I]
- Part D (Effect Size Sensitivity): (i) Cohen's d would decrease because larger SDs increase the pooled SD in the denominator; (ii) The decrease indicates less practical importance than the original findings. [Scored E/P/I]

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 6A) ===
A) Since p = 0.002 < alpha = 0.05, we reject Ho. There's convincing evidence for a difference in the mean reading score of children between reading at 9 am and reading at 3 pm.
B) The children were not matched up to a similar child or twin where one child from the pair reads in the morning and one reads in the afternoon, so a matched pairs would not be appropriate. The two groups were independent of each other, making a two-sample t-test appropriate.
C) i) Sp = sqrt((4.12^2 + 4.43^2)/2) = 4.2778. d = |15.2 - 17.9| / 4.2778 = 0.631.
ii) 0.631 is between 0.2 and 0.8, so it would be interpreted as somewhat meaningful in life. This means there is a somewhat important difference in the mean reading scores of children between reading in the morning and reading at night.
D) i) The Cohen's d coefficient in the new situation would be smaller than what was calculated in part C. This is because Sp would become greater... A larger Sp means a bigger denominator in Cohen's d coefficient formula resulting in a smaller answer.
ii) It would have less importance because Table 2 indicates that smaller Cohen's d coefficients correspond to less importance. Part D(i) talks of a smaller coefficient meaning less importance.
feedback:
Total Score: 4/4 points (Complete Response: Part A - E, Part B - E, Part C - E, Part D - E).
- Part A [E]: Compared p-value to alpha, rejected H0, and stated conclusion with non-definitive language in full context (means, groups, units, variable).
- Part B [E]: Stated groups are independent and provided a valid counter-example of how data could have been paired (matching twins).
- Part C [E]: Correctly calculated pooled SD (4.28) and Cohen's d (0.631), accurately interpreting it as 'somewhat meaningful in life'.
- Part D [E]: Correctly deduced Cohen's d decreases due to a larger denominator (pooled SD) and recognized this reflects less practical importance.

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics 1 2025 Question 1 (10 points total).
Topic: Mathematical Routines (Momentum Conservation, Kinetic Energy Loss & Internal Forces).
Problem Context: A cart of mass m_c travels with velocity v_c at t < t1. At t = t1, a block of mass m_b = (1/5)m_c is dropped onto the cart, sticking to it through inelastic collision until t2. System mass becomes (6/5)m_c.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A(i) [2 pts]: (A1) Constant p_x for t < t1 or t > t1; (A2) Continuous horizontal line across t = 0 to t2 (or beyond) indicating total momentum conservation.
- Part A(ii) [2 pts]: (A3) Include conservation of momentum equation p_i = p_f; (A4) Set m_c*v_c equal to (m_c + m_b)v_f and solve v_f = (5/6)v_c.
- Part A(iii) [3 pts]: (A5) Multi-step derivation with K = 1/2 m v^2; (A6) Initial mass m_c and final mass (6/5)m_c; (A7) Substitute v_f = (5/6)v_c to find Delta K = -(1/12) m_c v_c^2.
- Part B [3 pts]: (B1) Check 'Remains constant'; (B2) Indicate frictional force between block and cart is internal to system (Newton's 3rd Law pair); (B3) State net external force is zero, so total momentum is conserved.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 1A) ===
Part A: (i) [Continuous horizontal line drawn at constant p_x from t=0 to t2].
(ii) p_i = p_f -> m_c*v_c = (m_c + m_b)v_f = (m_c + (1/5)m_c)v_f = (6/5)m_c*v_f -> v_f = (5/6)v_c.
(iii) Delta K = K_f - K_i = 1/2(m_c + m_b)v_f^2 - 1/2 m_c v_c^2 = 1/2 (6/5 m_c)((5/6)v_c)^2 - 1/2 m_c v_c^2 = 5/12 m_c v_c^2 - 1/2 m_c v_c^2 = -1/12 m_c v_c^2. The system lost 1/12 m_c v_c^2 in kinetic energy.
Part B: [Check: Remains constant]. The block is dropped from rest onto the cart so the initial horizontal component of the block's momentum is zero. Additionally, the frictional force between the block and the cart is internal to the system, so it doesn't cause a change in momentum as only external forces change a system's momentum.

- Part A(ii) [2/2 pts]: Earned A3 for stating conservation of momentum and A4 for setting initial momentum equal to combined final momentum and solving v_f = (5/6)v_c[cite: 59].
- Part A(iii) [3/3 pts]: Earned A5, A6, and A7 for substituting initial/final masses and derived final velocity into kinetic energy difference, obtaining -(1/12)m_c*v_c^2[cite: 59].
- Part B [3/3 pts]: Earned B1 for selecting 'Remains constant', B2 for identifying friction as an internal force, and B3 for concluding zero net external force maintains constant momentum[cite: 59].

Exam: AP Physics 1 2025 Question 2 (12 points total).
Topic: Translation Between Representations (Mechanical Energy Bar Charts, Energy Conservation & Spring Oscillation).
Problem Context: Block of mass M released from rest at x = 0 on an incline of angle theta. At x = 6D, block is moving down the ramp. At x = 8D, it contacts an uncompressed spring of constant k. At x = 12D, the spring reaches max compression (Delta x = 4D) and block momentarily stops. Total mechanical energy E = 12E0. Baseline Ug = 0 at x = 12D.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A [3 pts]: (A1) Figure 2 (x=0) has single bar for Ug; (A2) Figure 3 (x=6D) has only K and Ug; (A3) Total height in Figure 2 and Figure 3 equals 12E0.
- Part B [4 pts]: (B1) Conservation of energy derivation; (B2) Equate max Ug to max Us; (B3) Substitute Delta y = 12D*sin(theta) and Delta x = 4D; (B4) Solve k = (3/2)(Mg*sin(theta)/D).
- Part C [3 pts]: (C1) Horizontal line at 12E0 from 8D to 12D labeled E; (C2) Straight decreasing line labeled Ug; (C3) Ug line starts at (8D, 4E0) and ends at (12D, 0).
- Part D [2 pts]: (D1) State v_9D > v_8D; (D2) Justify using energy graph: at x = 8D, Us = 0, Ug = 4E0 -> K = 8E0; at x = 9D, Us < E0, Ug = 3E0 -> K > 8E0, hence speed is greater.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 2A) ===
Part A: [Fig 2 at x=0: Ug = 12E0, K = 0, Us = 0. Fig 3 at x=6D: K = 6E0, Ug = 6E0, Us = 0].
Part B: Conservation of energy: Maximum Ug = Maximum Us -> mgh = 1/2 k x^2 -> Mg(12D sin(theta)) = 1/2 k (4D)^2 -> 12MgD sin(theta) = 8 k D^2 -> k = (3/2)(Mg sin(theta)/D).
Part C: [Fig 4: Horizontal line at E = 12E0 from 8D to 12D. Straight decreasing line Ug from (8D, 4E0) to (12D, 0)].
Part D: [Check: v_9D > v_8D]. The kinetic energy of the system at any position is equal to 12E0 (total mechanical energy) minus Ug and Us at that position, due to conservation of energy. At position 8D, the graph shows that Ug = 4E0 and Us = 0, while at position 9D, Ug = 3E0 and Us < E0. Since there is less total Ug and Us at 9D, there is more kinetic energy. K = 1/2 mv^2 and since the mass is constant, the velocity at the 9D mark is greater than at 8D.

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics 1 2025 Question 3 (10 points total).
Topic: Experimental Design and Analysis (Rotational Torque Equilibrium, Graphing Linearization & Mass Determination).
Problem Context: A uniform meterstick of mass M is pivoted at a stand. In Experiment 1, a block of unknown mass m0 is attached to the meterstick and balanced horizontally using a spring scale at the left end. In Experiment 2, a string pulls at angle theta to support the stick; tension F_T is recorded as a function of 1/sin(theta). Torque equation: F_T*sin(theta)*(5/6)L - Mg*(1/2)L = 0 -> F_T = (3/5)Mg / sin(theta).
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A [2 pts]: (A1) Procedure attaching block to meterstick and measuring force on left end with spring scale; (A2) Reduce uncertainty by repeating force measurements at multiple block locations.
- Part B [2 pts]: (B1) Plot Force F vs. distance d from pivot to block; (B2) Relate slope to m0: slope = (m0*g)/d_scale -> m0 = (slope*d_scale)/g.
- Part C [4 pts]: (C1) Plot F_T on vertical axis; (C2) Label vertical axis with linear scale and units (N); (C3) Correctly plot data points; (C4) Draw appropriate best-fit line.
- Part D [2 pts]: (D1) Relate slope to mass: slope = (3/5)Mg -> M = (5/3)(slope/g); (D2) Calculate mass M in range 0.90 kg to 1.15 kg.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 3A) ===
Part A: 1. Attach the block of mass m0 to the 90 cm mark of the meterstick. 2. Attach a spring scale to the 10 cm mark. Pull the scale until the meterstick is horizontal and record the force on the spring scale. Repeat this 3 times and average. 3. Repeat steps 1 & 2 but with the block at different holes of the meterstick (e.g. 50 cm, 70 cm, 80 cm marks).
Part B: In the experiment, net torque is zero. F_scale * d_scale = m0*g*d_block. Plot F_scale on the vertical axis and d_block on the horizontal axis. The slope of the graph is m0*g/d_scale. Thus m0 = slope * d_scale / g.
Part C: Vertical axis: F_T (N). Horizontal axis: 1/sin(theta). [Scale 0 to 25 N; data points plotted correctly; best-fit line drawn].
Part D: slope = 3/5 Mg = 5.88 N -> M = 5/3(slope)/g = 5(5.88)/(3*9.8) = 1.0 kg.

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics 1 2025 Question 4 (8 points total).
Topic: Qualitative Quantitative Translation (Fluid Buoyancy, Newton's Second Law & Functional Dependence).
Problem Context: Block of mass m and volume V submerged in freshwater (density rho1) in Scenario 1, and in saltwater (density rho2 > rho1) in Scenario 2. Block released from rest, accelerates upward.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A [3 pts]: (A1) Claim a1 < a2; (A2) State both blocks have identical downward gravitational force (weight mg); (A3) State saltwater exerts larger upward buoyant force F_B than freshwater because rho2 > rho1, resulting in larger net upward force.
- Part B [3 pts]: (B1) Multistep derivation starting with Newton's 2nd Law: Sigma F = ma; (B2) Substitute buoyant force F_B = rho*V*g; (B3) Solve initial upward acceleration: a = (rho*V*g - mg)/m = (rho*V*g)/m - g.
- Part C [2 pts]: (C1) Attempt to address functional dependence between a and rho; (C2) Correctly explain that derived equation shows a is proportional to rho through the positive (rho*V*g)/m term, confirming that higher fluid density rho2 yields greater acceleration a2 > a1.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 4A) ===
Part A: a1 < a2. The downward gravitational force (F_g = mg) is the same on both blocks because they have identical mass. The buoyant force is F_B = rho*V*g. Since saltwater is more dense (rho2 > rho1), the buoyant force in Scenario 2 is greater than in Scenario 1. With a greater net upward force in Scenario 2, the acceleration of Block 2 will be greater than Block 1 (a2 > a1).
Part B: Sigma F = ma -> F_B - F_g = ma -> rho*V*g - mg = ma -> a = (rho*V*g - mg)/m.
Part C: In part B, a = (rho*V*g - mg)/m. Since rho is located in the numerator, as density increases, acceleration increases. Since rho2 > rho1, the equation mathematically shows a2 > a1, which matches my claim in part A.
feedback:
Total Score: 8/8 points (Perfect Score: A1-1, A2-1, A3-1, B1-1, B2-1, B3-1, C1-1, C2-1)[cite: 62].

- Part B [3/3 pts]: Earned B1 for Newton's 2nd Law, B2 for F_B = rho*V*g, and B3 for correct acceleration expression[cite: 62].
- Part C [2/2 pts]: Earned C1 and C2 for evaluating functional dependence (a increases linearly with rho in the numerator) consistent with Part A[cite: 62].

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics 2 2025 Question 1 (10 points total).
Topic: Mathematical Routines (Magnetic Fields of Long Wires, Magnetic Force Equilibrium & Electromagnetic Induction).
Problem Context: Wire 1 carries current I in +x direction along y = 0. Wire 2 carries current I in +x direction at y = -d. Wire 3 carrying current 2I is placed along y3 to cancel the net magnetic force on Wire 1. A square loop above Wire 1 moves in +y direction.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A(i) [2 pts]: (A1) Magnetic field from Wire 2 at Point P on Wire 1 is into the page (X); (A2) Magnetic force on Wire 1 by Wire 2 is directed in +y direction (upward arrow).
- Part A(ii) [5 pts]: (A3) Multistep derivation using B = mu0*I/(2*pi*r) or Sigma F = 0; (A4) B2 = mu0*I/(2*pi*d); (A5) B3 = mu0*(2I)/(2*pi*|y3|); (A6) Equate B2 = B3; (A7) Solve y3 = -2d.
- Part B [3 pts]: (B1) State induced current in loop is Clockwise; (B2) State magnetic field inside loop due to wires 1 & 2 is directed into the page; (B3) Apply Lenz's Law: as loop moves away in +y, into-the-page flux decreases, inducing clockwise current to create into-the-page field.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 1A) ===
Part A: (i) Fig 2: [X (Into page)]. Fig 3: [Upward arrow (+y)].
(ii) F_B = I1*L*B_other = I1*L*(mu0*I_other / (2*pi*r)). For net force on Wire 1 to be zero: F_B2 + F_B3 = 0 -> F_B2 = -F_B3 -> I*L*(mu0*I/(2*pi*d)) = -I*L*(mu0*(-2I)/(2*pi*y3)) -> 1/d = -2/y3 -> y3 = -2d.
Part B: [Check: Clockwise]. The magnetic field from wires 1 and 2 in the region of the loop points in the -z direction (into page). As the loop moves in the +y direction, the magnetic field strength decreases, so the magnetic flux into the page decreases. By Lenz's law, an induced magnetic field is created in the -z direction to oppose the change, requiring a clockwise induced current.

- Part A(ii) [5/5 pts]: Earned A3 for force balance derivation, A4 for B2 expression, A5 for B3 with 2I, A6 for equating forces, and A7 for solving y3 = -2d[cite: 63].

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics 2 2025 Question 2 (12 points total).
Topic: Translation Between Representations (Gas Thermodynamics, Piston Free-Body Diagram & PV Graphs).
Problem Context: Cylinder with movable piston of mass M and area A contains ideal gas at volume V0 and temp T0 under atmospheric pressure P_atm. Piston in equilibrium. Gas then expands/compresses. Later, a block is placed on piston returning volume to V0.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A [3 pts]: Free-body diagram on piston: (A1) Downward arrow for gravity F_g = Mg; (A2) Downward arrow for atmosphere F_atm = P_atm*A; (A3) Upward arrow for gas F_gas = P*A.
- Part B [4 pts]: (B1) Multistep derivation using U = (3/2)nRT and Sigma F = 0; (B2) Relate internal energy to PV: U = (3/2)PV; (B3) Solve equilibrium absolute pressure: P = P_atm + Mg/A; (B4) Derive U = (3/2)(P_atm + Mg/A)V0.
- Part C [3 pts]: (C1) Curve connecting lower-right to upper-left; (C2) Curve is concave up; (C3) Arrow pointing leftward/upward (from larger to smaller volume / smaller to larger pressure).
- Part D [2 pts]: (D1) State T_new > T0; (D2) Justify: with extra block, equilibrium pressure P increases while volume returns to V0, so by ideal gas law (PV = nRT), temperature must increase.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 2A) ===
Part A: [FBD: Upward arrow labeled F_gas; downward arrow labeled F_g; downward arrow labeled F_atm].
Part B: U = 3/2 nRT, PV = nRT -> U = 3/2 P_gas V0. Equilibrium: F_gas = F_g + F_atm -> P_gas A = Mg + P_atm A -> P_gas = Mg/A + P_atm. Therefore U = 3/2 (Mg/A + P_atm) V0.
Part C: [Concave-up curve from lower-right to upper-left with arrow pointing up-left].
Part D: [Check: T_new > T0]. As seen in part A, the force of the gas balances the weight of the piston and atmospheric force. If the weight increases, F_gas must increase. F_gas = P_gas*A; since area did not change, gas pressure must increase. Since P is proportional to T for a constant volume V0, increasing pressure means temperature must increase (T_new > T0).

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics 2 2025 Question 3 (10 points total).
Topic: Experimental Design and Analysis (RC Circuit Time Constant & Capacitor Linearization).
Problem Context: Students determine expected time constant tau = R*C of a circuit with a square parallel-plate capacitor (side length s, plate area A = s^2, separation d) and resistor R. In Experiment 2, charge q is measured as a function of Delta V: q = C*Delta V.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A [2 pts]: (A1) Procedure to measure capacitor dimensions (side s, separation d) and resistor current I (using known battery emf); (A2) Reduce uncertainty by repeating measurements.
- Part B [2 pts]: (B1) State tau = R_eq * C_eq; (B2) State R = emf/I and C = epsilon0*A/d.
- Part C [4 pts]: (C1) Plot q vs. Delta V to produce linear graph; (C2) Linear scale with units (e.g. 10^-10 C and V); (C3) Plot data points accurately; (C4) Draw best-fit line approximating data.
- Part D [2 pts]: (D1) Relate slope to capacitance: slope = Delta q / Delta V = C; (D2) Compute C in acceptable range (7*10^-11 F to 9*10^-11 F, ~8*10^-11 F).

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 3A) ===
Part A: tau = R_eq * C_eq. To find R_eq, create a circuit with the battery, resistor, and ammeter in series. Do multiple trials and record the average current. To find capacitance, measure length of side of capacitor (s) to get Area A = s^2 with ruler, taking multiple readings and averaging. Then measure plate distance d with ruler, taking multiple readings.
Part B: Take average current from resistor measurement, divide battery voltage by this (R = V/I). Use area A and distance d to calculate C = epsilon0 * A / d. Then tau = R_eq * C_eq.
Part C: Vertical axis: q (x10^-10 C). Horizontal axis: |Delta V| (V). [Linear scales 0-12 V and 0-10x10^-10 C; points plotted; best-fit line drawn].
Part D: C = q/Delta V = slope = (7.35x10^-10 - 2x10^-10) / (9.1 - 2.4) = 8.1 x 10^-11 C/V. C = 8.1 x 10^-11 F.

Exam: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism 2025 Question 1 (10 points total).
Topic: Mathematical Routines (Gauss's Law for Cylinders, Potential Difference Integral & Cylindrical Capacitance with Dielectric).
Problem Context: Long coaxial cylinders. Inner conducting cylinder of radius R1 has surface charge density +sigma1. Outer conducting shell has inner radius R2. Length L >> R2.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A(i) [3 pts]: (A1) Multistep derivation with Gauss's Law oint E dot dA = q_enc / epsilon0; (A2) Gaussian cylinder area 2*pi*r*l; (A3) Enclosed charge q_enc = sigma1*(2*pi*R1*l), solving E(r) = (sigma1*R1) / (epsilon0*r).
- Part A(ii) [2 pts]: (A4) Substitute E into Delta V = -int E dot dr; (A5) Solve integral with limits R1 to R2: Delta V = (sigma1*R1/epsilon0) * ln(R2/R1).
- Part A(iii) [2 pts]: (A6) Sketch E = 0 for r < R1 and r > R2; (A7) Sketch decreasing concave-up curve for R1 < r < R2.
- Part B [3 pts]: (B1) Use C = Q / Delta V; (B2) State dielectric multiplies capacitance by kappa (C_d = kappa*C0); (B3) Substitute Q = sigma1*(2*pi*R1*L) and Delta V to derive C = (2*pi*kappa*epsilon0*L) / ln(R2/R1).

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 1A) ===
Part A: (i) oint E dot dA = q_enc / epsilon0 -> E(2*pi*r*l) = rho*(pi*R1^2*l)/epsilon0 -> E = (rho*R1^2)/(2*epsilon0*r) [Used volume charge density].
(ii) Delta V = int_R1^R2 E dr = int_R1^R2 (rho*R1^2)/(2*epsilon0*r) dr = (rho*R1^2)/(2*epsilon0) * ln(R2/R1).
(iii) [Graph: E=0 for 0 < r < R1; decreasing concave-up curve from R1 to R2; E=0 for r > R2].
Part B: C = Q / Delta V. With dielectric C = kappa*C_vac. Q = sigma1*(2*pi*R1*L). Substituting Delta V gives C = (2*pi*kappa*epsilon0*L) / ln(R2/R1).

Exam: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism 2025 Question 1 (Gauss's Law & Cylindrical Capacitors).
Rubric Requirements: Gauss's Law derivation (Part Ai); Potential difference integral (Part Aii); E(r) graph (Part Aiii); Capacitance with dielectric (Part B).

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 1B) ===
Part A: (i) oint E dot dA = q_enc/epsilon0 -> E(2*pi*r*l) = sigma1*(pi*R1^2*l)/epsilon0 -> E = (sigma1*R1^2)/(2*epsilon0*r).
(ii) |Delta V| = int_R1^R2 E dr = (sigma1*R1^2)/(2*epsilon0) * ln(R2/R1).
(iii) [Graph: E=0 for r < R1; decreasing concave-up curve for R1 < r < R2; E=0 for r > R2].
Part B: C = kappa*epsilon0*A/d = kappa*epsilon0*(pi*R2^2*L)/(R2 - R1).
feedback:
Total Score: 6/10 points (A1-1, A2-1, A3-0, A4-1, A5-1, A6-1, A7-1, B1-0, B2-0, B3-0)[cite: 66].
- Part A(i) [2/3 pts]: Earned A1 and A2, missed A3 for using area pi*R1^2 instead of 2*pi*R1*l for enclosed surface charge[cite: 66].
- Part A(ii) [2/2 pts]: Earned A4 and A5 for consistent integration of derived field[cite: 66].
- Part A(iii) [2/2 pts]: Earned A6 and A7 for correct graph[cite: 66].
- Part B [0/3 pts]: Failed all; applied parallel-plate formula C = kappa*epsilon0*A/d instead of deriving from C = Q/Delta V for coaxial cylinders[cite: 66].

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics C: Mechanics 2025 Question 1 (10 points total).
Topic: Mathematical Routines (1D Momentum Vector Diagrams, Impulse Integral & Completely Inelastic Collision).
Problem Context: Block 1 (mass m) moves right at +2v0 (p1 = +2mv0). Block 2 (mass 6m) moves left at -v0 (p2 = -6mv0). Total initial momentum p_tot = -4mv0. Blocks collide with interaction force F(t) = F_max*sin(A*t) for 0 <= t <= t_c where A*t_c = pi, sticking together at final velocity v_f = -4/7 v0.
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A(i) [2 pts]: (A1) Draw Block 2 initial momentum arrow pointing left with length 6 units; (A2) Draw two-block system before & after momentum arrows pointing left with length 4 units.
- Part A(ii) [5 pts]: (A3) Impulse integral J = int F(t) dt = Delta p; (A4) Delta p for Block 2 = 6m(-4/7 v0 - (-v0)) = +18/7 mv0 (or Block 1 Delta p = -18/7 mv0); (A5) Substitute F_max*sin(At); (A6) Integrate with limits 0 to t_c yielding (2*F_max)/A; (A7) Solve F_max = (9*A*m*v0) / (7*(1 - cos(A*t_c))) = (9/7) A m v0.
- Part B [3 pts]: (B1) Momentum conservation for new initial speed v1: p_i = p_f; (B2) Set magnitude of final momentum equal to 7m*v0 (moving right at +v0); (B3) Solve m*v1 + 6m(-v0) = +7m*v0 -> v1 = 13v0.

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 1A) ===
Part A: (i) [Fig 2: Block 2 drawn 6 units left. Two-block before drawn 4 units left; Two-block after drawn 4 units left].
(ii) Delta p = int_0^t_c F_net dt = int_0^t_c F_max*sin(A*t) dt = -F_max/A * cos(At) |_0^t_c = F_max/A (1 - cos(A*t_c)). For Block 2: m1*v1 + m2*v2 = (m1 + m2)v_f -> 2mv0 - 6mv0 = 7m*v_f -> v_f = -4/7 v0. Delta p2 = 6m(-4/7 v0 - (-v0)) = 18/7 mv0. Setting equal: F_max/A (1 - cos(A*t_c)) = 18/7 mv0 -> F_max = (18 A m v0) / [7(1 - cos(A*t_c))].
Part B: p_i = p_f -> m1*v1 + m2*v2 = (m1 + m2)v_f -> m*v1 + 6m(-v0) = (m + 6m)v0 -> m*v1 - 6mv0 = 7mv0 -> v1 = 13v0.
feedback:
Total Score: 10/10 points (Perfect Score: A1-1, A2-1, A3-1, A4-1, A5-1, A6-1, A7-1, B1-1, B2-1, B3-1)[cite: 67].
- Part A(i) [2/2 pts]: Earned A1 for 6-unit leftward vector for Block 2 and A2 for identical 4-unit leftward vectors for total system before and after[cite: 67].
- Part A(ii) [5/5 pts]: Earned A3 for impulse integral, A4 for Delta p = 18/7 mv0, A5 for sine force substitution, A6 for definite integration, and A7 for exact F_max expression[cite: 67].
- Part B [3/3 pts]: Earned B1 for momentum conservation, B2 for +7mv0 final momentum, and B3 for solving v1 = 13v0[cite: 67].

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics C: Mechanics 2025 Question 1 (1D Momentum & Impulse Integration).
Rubric Requirements: Vector diagram (Part Ai); F_max impulse derivation (Part Aii); v1 momentum conservation (Part B).

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 1B) ===
Part A: (i) [Block 2: 6 units left. Two-block before: 4 units left. Two-block after: 4 units left].
(ii) Impulse = Delta p = int F dt -> int_0^t_c F_max*sin(At) dt = -F_max/A * cos(A*t_c) + F_max/A. Delta p = -4mv0 - 0 = -4mv0. Setting equal: F_max(1 - cos(At_c))/A = 4mv0 -> F_max = 4mv0*A / (1 - cos(At_c)).
Part B: m1*v1 + m2*v2 = (m1 + m2)v_f -> m*v1 - 2mv0 = 3m(v0) -> v1 = 5v0.
feedback:
Total Score: 6/10 points (A1-1, A2-1, A3-1, A4-0, A5-1, A6-1, A7-0, B1-1, B2-0, B3-0)[cite: 67].
- Part A(i) [2/2 pts]: Earned A1 and A2 for correct momentum arrows[cite: 67].
- Part A(ii) [3/5 pts]: Earned A3, A5, and A6 for correct impulse integration, missed A4 (used -4mv0 instead of individual block change 18/7 mv0) and A7 (incorrect F_max)[cite: 67].
- Part B [1/3 pts]: Earned B1 for momentum conservation setup, missed B2 (used 3mv0 instead of 7mv0) and B3 (derived v1 = 5v0 instead of 13v0)[cite: 67].

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics C: Mechanics 2025 Question 2 (12 points total).
Topic: Translation Between Representations (Coupled Oscillator Energy Bar Charts, SHM Speed Derivation & Damped Oscillations).
Problem Context: Block of mass m on frictionless surface connected to Spring A (constant k) and Spring B (constant 2k). Equilibrium at x = 0. Block displaced to x = x1 and released from rest. Later, block undergoes damped SHM with friction on a rough surface (Scenario 2), then tested with larger mass (Scenario 3).
Rubric Expectations:
- Part A [3 pts]: (A1) K_block = 0 at x = x1; (A2) U_A and U_B bars both have positive heights; (A3) Height of U_B bar is twice the height of U_A bar (U_B = 1/2(2k)x1^2 = 2*U_A).
- Part B [4 pts]: (B1) Conservation of energy or SHM derivation; (B2) Include both spring constants (k_eff = 3k); (B3) Relate initial position x1 and intermediate position (1/2)x1; (B4) Derive speed v = (3/2)x1*sqrt(k/m) or (1/2)x1*sqrt(3k/m).
- Part C [3 pts]: (C1) Curve starts at zero and remains >= 0 for all t; (C2) Zeros spaced periodically with period (1/2)T; (C3) Successive peaks exhibit decreasing amplitude.
- Part D [2 pts]: (D1) State period T increases (or peak amplitudes decrease faster); (D2) Justify: T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k_eff), so increasing mass m increases period (or greater mass increases normal force F_N = mg, increasing friction work W_f = mu*mg*d and damping rate).

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 2A) ===
Part A: [Fig 3: U_A = 2 units, U_B = 4 units, K_block = 0].
Part B: Energy is conserved: E_tot = 1/2 k_eff A^2, where k_eff = k_A + k_B = 3k. Initial state at x1: E_tot = 1/2(3k)x1^2. At x = 1/2 x1: E_tot = U_A + U_B + K -> 1/2(3k)x1^2 = 1/2 k (1/2 x1)^2 + 1/2(2k)(1/2 x1)^2 + 1/2 m v^2 -> 3/2 k x1^2 = 3/8 k x1^2 + 1/2 m v^2 -> 9/8 k x1^2 = 1/2 m v^2 -> v = sqrt(9k x1^2 / (4m)) = 3/2 x1 sqrt(k/m).
Part C: [Fig 5: Periodic curve starting at (0,0), nonnegative, zeros at 1/2 T, T, 3/2 T, 2T..., with exponentially decaying peak amplitudes].
Part D: For Scenario 3, the peaks on the graph would be lower than in Part C. Friction force is F_fr = mu*F_N = mu*m*g. Greater mass m means greater F_fr, which does more negative work W_fr. This leads to a larger decrease in kinetic energy per period, so the peaks are lower.
feedback:
Total Score: 12/12 points (Perfect Score: A1-1, A2-1, A3-1, B1-1, B2-1, B3-1, B4-1, C1-1, C2-1, C3-1, D1-1, D2-1)[cite: 68].
- Part A [3/3 pts]: Earned A1 for K=0, A2 for positive U_A & U_B bars, and A3 for U_B height being exactly twice U_A[cite: 68].
- Part B [4/4 pts]: Earned B1 for energy conservation, B2 for k_eff = 3k, B3 for position substitution at x1/2, and B4 for exact speed derivation[cite: 68].
- Part C [3/3 pts]: Earned C1 for non-negative graph starting at origin, C2 for zeros at T/2 intervals, and C3 for decreasing peak amplitude[cite: 68].
- Part D [2/2 pts]: Earned D1 for lower peaks and D2 for linking increased mass to higher normal force, friction work, and energy dissipation rate[cite: 68].

=== QUESTION & RUBRIC CONTEXT ===
Exam: AP Physics C: Mechanics 2025 Question 2 (Oscillator Representations & Damped SHM).
Rubric Requirements: Energy bars (Part A); Speed derivation at x1/2 (Part B); Damped kinetic energy curve (Part C); Effect of mass on damped oscillation (Part D).

=== STUDENT RESPONSE (SAMPLE 2B) ===
Part A: [Fig 3: U_A = -2 units, U_B = 2 units, K_block = 0].
Part B: U = 1/2 kx^2, K = 1/2 mv^2. 1/2(2k)(1/2 x1)^2 + 1/2(k)(1/2 x1)^2 + 1/2 mv^2 = 1/2 k x1^2 + 1/2 k x1^2 -> 1/4 k x1^2 + 1/8 k x1^2 + 1/2 mv^2 = k x1^2 -> 3/8 k x1^2 + 1/2 mv^2 = k x1^2 -> 1/2 mv^2 = 5/8 k x1^2 -> v = sqrt(5k x1^2 / (4m)).
Part C: [Fig 5: Starts at (0, 4), drops below t-axis into negative values, zeros spaced at T/2, decreasing amplitude].
Part D: The period of each oscillation will increase because according to T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k), period is positively related to mass m, so increasing mass increases period.
feedback:
Total Score: 8/12 points (A1-1, A2-0, A3-0, B1-1, B2-1, B3-1, B4-0, C1-0, C2-1, C3-1, D1-1, D2-1)[cite: 68].
- Part A [1/3 pts]: Earned A1 for K=0, missed A2 (drew negative bar for U_A) and A3 (drew equal magnitudes)[cite: 68].
- Part B [3/4 pts]: Earned B1, B2, and B3 for energy conservation setup with both springs at x1/2, missed B4 due to right-hand side spring constant error[cite: 68].
- Part C [2/3 pts]: Earned C2 for T/2 zero intervals and C3 for decreasing amplitude, missed C1 because graph started above zero and dipped negative[cite: 68].
- Part D [2/2 pts]: Earned D1 for period increase and D2 for citing T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) dependence on mass[cite: 68].
